> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Changes are confined to research documentation and JSON finite-check receipts; they correct theoretical scope and do not alter application runtime, auth, or data paths.
> 
> **Overview**
> This PR **tightens and extends** the Grand GMI research package: it repairs several over-strong implications, adds constructive finite-horizon laws, and versions executable receipts (master **V4**, coverage/morphology **V2**, new green JSON payloads).
> 
> **Acquisition and control.** Epistemic claims are scoped so full protected-response identification (`eta_Omega`) is separate from **task-directed** stopping on compatible successful actions (TDA-1–3), with an explicit experiment/memory tradeoff frontier. **CRA-1–3** adds configuration-level belief updates, least-fixed-point terminating-policy synthesis, and finite-horizon control costs (linked from ACL and controlled acquisition). Controlled-acquisition evidence moves to **receipt V2** with policy-computed CA-5 values.
> 
> **Selection, phase laws, and coverage.** **MSC-1–3** require a **nonempty** selected set before architecture properties are derived, finite constructive coverage for attained Pareto frontiers, complete profile fibers, and interval exclusion with **eta-suboptimal** witnesses when optima are unattained—propagated through morphology selection, family phase, ACL-7, DRS, and AR ledgers. Morphology phase derivation is rewritten for **overcharging** accounting failures, scoped **PL-5** insufficiency (with a documented positive exception), and **receipt V2**. Candidate-universe coverage drops a universal “decidable coverage” claim in favor of **finite enumeration**, supplied proof certificates, and a **nonhalting** boundary (**CU-1b**); reporting now distinguishes population-wide verdicts from covered-class scope.
> 
> **New modules and narrowed separation.** Adds theorems for **certified reuse after invalidation** (CRI), **empirical frontier identification** under joint uncertainty (EFI), and **mutual nondetermination** of full partition-width vs query summaries (FPW). The information–computation separation document is **narrowed** to final-cut width vs deterministic query depth, with FPW as the stronger width/query successor. A new **CORE.md** indexes these additions; master theory and closure ledgers point at it and the scientific queue.
> 
> Receipt stack grows (controlled relational acquisition, reuse invalidation, partition width, empirical frontier, selection attainment, candidate coverage V2, etc.) with source-bound checker hashes in **GRAND_GMI_MASTER_RECEIPT_V4.json**.

Owner-requested (2026-09-13): `aira top` should show each job's age.

**Format** (owner rule): the most-significant non-zero unit + the next unit below it, dropping the second when it is zero:

| Age | Shown |
|---|---|
| 1d2h3m4s | `1d2h` |
| 1d0h5m | `1d` |
| 2h0m4s | `2h` |
| 2h3m4s | `2h3m` |
| 3m4s | `3m4s` |
| 45s | `45s` |
| 0s | `0s` |

Days are computed locally (`time.Duration.String` has no day unit). Data was already present — `ConfineRecord.AgeSeconds` (from S1); `nil`/negative → `"unevaluated"`, never `"0s"` (the table's honesty convention). `confine --list` keeps its existing wide Go-duration rendering (`confineAge`); only the TUI table gets the compact column.

Also makes the reserve test's positional cell lookup **header-relative**, so a future column insertion cannot silently shift which cell it reads.

author: aicountly
body:
The **production** dry run for company 3 listed `inv_audit_log` (2 rows) among the tables it would delete. The sandbox never showed this, because company 3 had already been purged there before the fix existed.

Books retains its audit trail for eight years — `AuditRetentionRegistry::mayPurge()` returns `false`, and a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger enforces it. Deleting Inventory's would leave a purged company's history **half preserved and half destroyed**, which is worse than either answer on its own. Inventory owns the stock domain Books used to own, and the audit of that domain lives here now; the two halves are one record.

## Change

`inv_audit_log` and `inv_access_audit_log` are retained: not deleted, and not copied into the archive schema (that schema is dropped after 30–90 days, so copying records meant to outlive it would only duplicate them on their way out).

For company 3 this moves 2 rows from "deleted" to "retained". Small in volume, but the principle decides what happens to every company purged after this one.

## What this does not do

Nothing enforces append-only on this side. `AuditService` calls `inv_audit_log` append-only in its docblock and no trigger backs that up, unlike Books. Adding one belongs in a migration of its own — it would start rejecting writes that exist today, which is not something to discover partway through a purge. Until that exists, `RETAINED` is what stands between a deleted company and its audit trail.

`appendOnlyTables()` still reads `pg_trigger` on every run, so if such a migration lands later and misses a table, the purge stops rather than deleting it.

**Follow-up worth filing:** harden `inv_audit_log` / `inv_access_audit_log` with the same trigger Books uses, and give Inventory an equivalent of `AuditRetentionRegistry` so the retention period is stated in one place rather than implied by a purge command's constant.

## Verification

Full suite green: 82 tests, 860 assertions, including a new case asserting the audit rows stay in `public`, stay out of the archive, and are never the subject of a `DELETE`.

author: rushikeshgarad2024-dev
body:
## Description
Implements complete optional Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP, RFC 6238) lifecycle with encrypted secret storage at rest, single-use recovery backup codes, and login challenge handling.

## Key Changes
- **TOTP Engine (`src/auth/utils/totp.util.ts`)**:
  - RFC 6238 HMAC-SHA1 TOTP generation & verification with window drift support.
  - Standard Base32 secret generation and `otpauth://` QR URI generation (compatible with Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password).
  - AES-256-CBC secret encryption at rest.
  - 8 single-use 8-character backup recovery codes stored hashed via SHA-256.
- **User Entity (`src/auth/entities/user.entity.ts`)**:
  - Added `isTwoFactorEnabled` (boolean), `twoFactorSecret` (encrypted string), and `twoFactorBackupCodes` (hashed string array).
- **Endpoints (`src/auth/auth.controller.ts` & `src/auth/auth.service.ts`)**:
  - `POST /auth/2fa/setup`: Generates TOTP secret, QR URI, and 8 recovery backup codes.
  - `POST /auth/2fa/enable`: Verifies initial code to activate 2FA.
  - `POST /auth/login`: Returns `{ requires2FA: true, userId, message }` challenge when 2FA is active.
  - `POST /auth/2fa/verify`: Validates TOTP code or single-use recovery code and issues JWT access & refresh tokens upon success (consuming used backup code).
  - `POST /auth/2fa/disable`: Deactivates 2FA and securely clears stored credentials upon code validation.
- **Unit Tests (`src/auth/auth.2fa.spec.ts`)**:
  - Full test suite covering TOTP generation/verification, secret encryption/decryption roundtrip, backup codes, setup, enable, 2FA login challenge, verification, and deactivation.

Closes #78

author: abddssh
marknygaard
body:
Doc-only. ARCHITECTURE said nothing about API authentication, so
building it would have meant deciding by writing code — and this repo's
own rule is to fix the spec first. **Review this before I write the
Rust**, because it is the design.

## The shape

**Why a login at all** — not because the network is hostile. Satellites
will go on streaming to Wyoming unauthenticated and MQTT is untouched.
It is that a house has more than one person in it, and voice has known
who is speaking since speaker recognition shipped while the web surface
did not.

**GitHub is the front door, not the boundary.** Accounts there are free,
so "has a GitHub account" tests nothing. The boundary is a list in
config:

```toml
[auth]
github_client_id_env = "NILES_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID"
github_client_secret_env = "NILES_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET"
allowed = [
  { email = "you@example.com",     speaker = "mark" },
  { email = "someone@example.com", speaker = "majse" },
]
```

**No invite emails.** Adding a person is an edit, so there is no message
to send, no token to mint, no expiry to track, and no mail server to
configure for a household of two. That also drops the equivalent of
ai-harness's `invites.rs` + `invites_routes.rs` + `mail.rs` (~800 lines)
before it is written.

**`speaker` ties the two identities together**, so the person who says
"I am Mark" and the person holding the phone are one person sharing one
memory, rather than Niles keeping two.

**Matched on the address GitHub verified** — from `/user/emails`, never
the profile's `email` field, which is whatever the account holder typed.

## Borrowed from ai-harness

The security details, not the volume — `github_sso.rs` and `sso_flow.rs`
had already argued this through:

- Its `Audience::Existing` mode is exactly this model: never create an
  account, so the allowlist is the whole boundary.
- GitHub's OAuth app flow has no ID token to verify, so the callback is
  authenticated by a **single-use expiring `state`** *plus* a **cookie
  binding the attempt to the browser that began it**. Both, or refuse.
- Same-origin-only redirect after sign-in, rejecting `\`, control
  characters and `//` rather than trying to out-guess the URL parser.

## Recorded as separate: whether to expose Niles at all

This makes exposure possible, not necessary. Worth having in the spec
because it is easy to assume otherwise: **web push needs no inbound
port.** The subscription lives on Apple's or Google's service and Niles
only posts to it outbound, so a timer reaches a phone anywhere without
Niles being reachable from anywhere. WireGuard stays a real alternative.

## Deliberately not

No roles, no admin screens, no passwords, no reset flow, no second
factor, no sign-up. Two people in a house are both trusted with the
house, and the account Niles trusts is the GitHub one.

## Still open

- Whether to expose Niles externally at all.
- What Majse's verified GitHub address actually is (GitHub → Settings →
  Emails). If her account only has a `@users.noreply.github.com`
  address, that is what the list has to hold — or she verifies a real
  one first.

author: ser-vasilich
body:
Removing rows meant `(set t (select {from: t where: <negated>}))`, which binds
a new table — and a fresh table starts without the key map from #512, so the
next batch rebuilt it over every row. Requested in #511.

```clojure
(delete {from: 'levels where: (== instrument inst_)})   ;; in place, map kept
(delete {from: levels  where: (== instrument inst_)})   ;; a new table
```

Both forms evaluate the predicate once and compact the same matched-row list
with the same code. `where:` is required. A quoted symbol always rebinds and
answers with the symbol, in place or not.

**Compaction** is a memmove of the runs between deleted rows. Every column
type stores a fixed-width element — a `RAY_STR` cell is a 16-byte descriptor
and the pool it points into does not move with the row — so no column needs a
per-cell path. Row order survives, so a sorted column stays sorted; an
attached accelerator index does not, and is dropped.

**The map is patched, not rebuilt.** Compaction moves a surviving row from `r`
to `r - (deletions before r)` and changes no key, so every entry keeps its
bucket and only the row number it stores shifts — one pass over the slot
array, no hashing and no key reads. Entries naming a deleted row become
tombstones; clearing a slot would truncate the probe chain and orphan whatever
was displaced past it. Tombstones are counted, or the array could fill and the
free-slot scan in `upsert_map_put` would not terminate. A deletion of half the
table or more is handed to the next upsert to rebuild.

## Numbers

Three release builds — `master`, the parent branch, this one — on the shape
from #511: 245 313 rows, 494 batches of 497, 360 instruments, `(sym, sym,
i64)` key. Nine fingerprint fields including `sum(i * sz[i])`, which any
reordering would change. Byte-identical across all three in every mode.

`delete` against the idiom it replaces, same output:

| resets | `select` + rebind | `delete` |
|---|---:|---:|
| every 50th batch | 384 ms | 370 ms |
| every 10th, serial | 556 ms | 439 ms |
| every 10th, workers | 608 ms | 487 ms |

Non-delete path unchanged: 352 ms parent, 342 ms here.

## Tests

`test/rfl/table/delete.rfl` — both forms, no-match, deleting every row, string
and symbol columns, order preservation, errors, rebinding when the gate
misses, and seven shapes of the map patch: runs of adjacent deletions at the
start, middle and end, two runs, scattered, three single deletions in a row,
repeated deletes.

Each checked by sabotaging the patch. Two earlier versions were vacuous:
upserting all N keys back exceeds the load factor and forces a rebuild that
hides a bad patch, and deleting every second row is exactly half, which trips
the hand-to-rebuild rule. Both traps are noted in the file.

3785/3785 under ASan, with workers and serially.

Based on `fix/alter-inplace` (#525), itself on `perf/upsert-key-index` (#512).
Merge order: #512, #525, this.

author: spdrman
body:
Closes #810

Part of EPIC L phase 1, on top of the merged L1 (#808). Sibling of L2 (#809).

## What this is

A `NAME.remote.sh` runs on the host a backup set pulls from. The obvious implementation is to reuse the SFTP connection and ask it to run a command, and that implementation is wrong: `docs/ssh-setup.md` tells operators to force the backup account into `internal-sftp`, and such an account answers an exec request with `This service allows sftp connections only.` and exits 1. A forced-command account (`command=`, `ForceCommand`) is worse — it **accepts** the request, runs somebody else's program, and **exits 0**. An executor trusting that status would report a "quiesce the database" hook as successful when it never ran, and then back up a live database.

So the execution connection is modelled separately from the transfer connection, and exec capability is **proven per run** rather than declared.

## Resolution

`workflows.exec_connections` declares named execution connections, each carrying a whole `remote` block — host, port, user, the `File`/`Env`/`Command` credential reference, `known_hosts`, `max_connections`, `sensitive_endpoint`. `remote_exec_connection_ref` resolves either to one of those, or to a backup set spelled `source/set`, meaning "reuse that set's own source connection". A declared id may not contain `/`, so the order is unambiguous rather than arbitrary. There is deliberately **no** field for a shell, a sudo user or a command prefix: a hook runs as the configured SSH user and this product never escalates.

## Preflight, per run, before a byte of the hook is sent

1. the host identity matches the pinned `known_hosts` (knownhosts' own callback over the file the transport verifies against);
2. the exec channel is permitted **and ran our bytes** — proven by requiring a marker in the probe's own output, which neither `internal-sftp` nor a forced command can produce;
3. bash is present and executable at the configured path (127/126 become capability refusals naming the path, never a silent fall back to `/bin/sh`);
4. no PTY was allocated — asserted from inside the probe, because "we did not ask for one" is a statement about the client;
5. the captured bytes parse under the **target's own** `bash -n`, where the line numbers are the script's own.

A refusal fails the remote hook. Artifact backup over the same credential is untouched, and one test asserts both halves against one account.

## The envelope, shared with #809

New `core/internal/workflowexec` holds exactly what the two executors must not differ on, agreed with L2 over hub before either started: a fixed bash path, `--noprofile --norc`, **nothing injected** (no `-e`, `-u`, `-o pipefail`, `-x`), a sanitized baseline with `BASH_ENV`/`ENV`/`SHELLOPTS`/`BASHOPTS` cleared, NUL refused everywhere, and stdout/stderr as two logical streams whose chunks carry sequence numbers from **one** counter so the interleaving stays recoverable.

Remote-specific:

- the fixed remote command is `exec <bash> --noprofile --norc -s <token>` and carries nothing else, because the remote command line is world-readable in the remote process list. The bash path and the token are held to character rules and **refused rather than quoted**.
- the environment and the script travel on the channel's **stdin** as single-quoted shell literals. No `SendEnv`/`AcceptEnv` dependency (a hardened sshd refuses env requests), no upload, no here-document (bash implements one with a temp file), and therefore no file on the remote host at any point.

## Termination

Without a PTY, closing a channel does not reliably kill what was behind it — measured, not assumed. So: an exec-channel signal request, then a **reaper** session that kills the step's process **group** by its token (with a guard so a malformed `ps` line can never produce `kill -TERM -1`), then closing the channel. Certainty is one rule: `confirmed` iff the session completed — exit reported and both streams at EOF. That is what makes a deliberately detached descendant come out `unconfirmed` without a special case: it keeps stdout open, so nothing can be proved, and this product says so instead of claiming a clean stop.

Transport loss never produces an exit code: `Result.ExitCode` is a `*int` and the audit line prints `exit=unobserved`.

## Custody

`sftpConfig`'s credential switch is extracted into `resolveSourceCredential` and exported as `SourceSigner`/`SourceKnownHostsFile`, so the exec client applies the identical rules a transfer does (the one-of-three rule, #293's mode check, #311's directory chain, #298's at-rest decryption, #269's passphrase). The one property an exec client cannot keep — `key_file` never entering this process's memory — is recorded in the ADR rather than glossed, because it is a real if small widening.

## Evidence

`core/tests/sshexecintegration` against a real sshd (`scripts/e2e/exec-host.Dockerfile`) with four accounts differing only in what the server lets them run, reached through `core/tests/machines` (new `ExecHost` fixture, same watchdog/lease/image policy as the source machine; wired into `scripts/ci-local.sh` both ways the tier guard requires):

| what | test |
|---|---|
| SFTP-only refused for exec while the same credential lists artifacts | `TestAnSFTPOnlyAccountIsRefusedExecAndStillBacksUp` |
| forced command refused (exits 0, runs something else) | `TestAForcedCommandAccountIsRefusedExec` |
| exec-capable passes; no PTY; no contamination; syntax checked | `TestAnExecCapableAccountPassesPreflight` |
| missing bash refused, never substituted | `TestAMissingBashIsRefusedRatherThanSubstituted` |
| `bash -n` on the target refuses before line 1 runs | `TestASyntaxErrorIsCaughtOnTheTargetBeforeTheHookRuns` |
| host-key mismatch refuses, with a positive control | `TestAHostKeyPolicyViolationRefusesBeforeTheHookRuns` |
| separate streams, one increasing sequence, real exit code | `TestAHookRunsWithSeparateStreamsAndOneSequence` |
| hostile env values byte-identical by SHA-256 round trip, and inert | `TestHostileEnvironmentValuesArriveByteForByteAndAreNeverInterpreted` |
| no secret in the remote process list while the hook runs | `TestNoEnvironmentValueReachesTheRemoteProcessList` |
| nothing left on the remote host (searched, not listing-diffed) | `TestNothingIsLeftOnTheRemoteHost` |
| `~/.bashrc` cannot reach a hook | `TestShellStartupFilesDoNotChangeAHook` |
| a server-set `BASH_ENV` is refused | `TestBASHENVContaminationIsDetectedByThePreflight` |
| timeout and cancel of a foreground child → `confirmed`, process gone | `TestAForegroundHookIsTerminatedWithConfirmedCertainty`, `TestCancellingAForegroundHookIsAlsoConfirmed` |
| a detached child → `unconfirmed` | `TestADeliberatelyDetachedChildIsUnconfirmed` |
| a dropped connection is not an exit code | `TestTransportLossIsNotReportedAsAnExitCode` |
| audit line carries the facts and no credential | `TestTheAuditLineDescribesTheStepAndNoCredential` |
| a key file the deployment no longer owns exclusively is refused | `TestAKeyFileTheDeploymentNoLongerOwnsIsRefused` |

Plus unit suites: the payload is asserted by **parsing it back** under single-quote semantics (a substring assertion cannot express "no value became syntax"), and that assertion was checked non-vacuous by breaking `ShellQuote` and watching it fail.

## Verification

- `go test -race ./internal/transport/... ./service/... ./internal/workflow/... ./internal/workflowexec/... ./internal/remoteexec/...` — all green
- `go test -race ./tests/sshexecintegration/` — green (69s, container up and torn down in-test, no silent skip)
- `gofmt` clean on everything touched; `go vet` clean; `check_package_doc.py` regenerated for the two new packages

Pre-existing reds at this base, unrelated: `internal/testtier`'s ledger flags `internal/backupengine/source/sftp_test.go` (already moved on current `main`), and `internal/transport/rclone/backends_test.go` is gofmt-dirty on `main` too.

## Out of scope

Stage sequencing, cleanup and rec

author: kla-bemindlabs
body:
The request to stop was one process-wide flag, because a signal is. Right for Ctrl-C, wrong for everything else: `drain --workers` runs several runs at once, and a browser with a run in more than one pane wants to stop **one** of them — which a single flag can't express, and is why the browser refuses a second run.

## `Stop`

`ostraka_adapter::interrupt::Stop` — a per-run handle that answers yes to **its own request or the process-wide one**. Ctrl-C still stops everything.

It's cloned into everything one run launches:

| | |
|---|---|
| `ProcessAdapter::stopped_by` | the vendor session polls it |
| `gate::run_checks_until` / `run_command_until` | the checks poll it |
| `route::select_until` / `orchestrator::run_task_until` | bind it to one run |

**All additive.** `select`, `run_task`, `run_checks` and `run_command` keep their signatures and delegate with a fresh `Stop` — nothing downstream changed, no published signature moved.

## Two things found on the way

**An unbounded check couldn't be stopped at all.** With no `timeout_secs`, the gate waited on the child outright — no loop, so neither a stop nor Ctrl-C could reach it. It polls now.

**A flaky test, fixed at the root.** `milestone_one`'s stopped-run test set the process-wide flag while the binary's other tests ran in parallel, interrupting whatever run was going. That's why the two-runs test here passed alone and failed in the full file — and why `several_runs_at_once_do_not_collide` failed CI on #43, a change that didn't touch it. It now stops its run through its own `Stop`; that binary no longer touches the global flag, and **5 consecutive full runs are green**.

## Tests

- one vendor stopped, another finishes (adapter)
- Ctrl-C still stops a run that has its own stop (adapter)
- a check with no ceiling can be stopped (gate)
- **end to end:** two runs at once through routing, orchestrator and gate — one stopped → `Interrupted`, the other → approved

The browser change that uses this — each pane running its own task, `s` stopping only its pane — follows as its own PR.

`cargo fmt` · `cargo clippy -D warnings` · `cargo test --workspace` · `check-hygiene.sh` — green.

author: melroysaldanha
body:
The action tests stub npm, so they prove the action no longer asks npm to run from the checkout, not what npm would do if it did. docs/INVARIANTS.md said outright that nothing in the repository pinned the two attack routes v0.6.1 closed: a committed .npmrc repointing the registry, and a planted copy in the head's node_modules winning the resolution. This pins them against real npm.

bench/action-install.mjs starts two local registries on 127.0.0.1 (a legitimate one serving tarballs packed from this worktree's own packages, and a hostile one serving a marked fake at the same exact version), builds a fixture checkout as a real git repository carrying a hostile .npmrc and a planted node_modules copy with the fixture's node_modules/.bin first on PATH, and runs the action's real install and run steps, extracted from action.yml with the same helper the test suite uses, under real npm with GITHUB_WORKSPACE at the fixture and RUNNER_TEMP and HOME in fresh temp dirs. No network: every request goes to one of the two local servers, and both log what they receive.

The committed baseline records six cases. The current action.yml, in all three scenarios (npmrc plus planted copy, npmrc only, scoped npmrc only): the hostile registry receives zero requests, neither marker fires, the scanner that ran is the one installed under the runner temp prefix at 0.6.0, and the SARIF is the real scanner's. The pre-fix action.yml, read from git at v0.6.0 at run time: the planted copy runs, or the hostile registry serves the scanner, and the gate exits 0. That negative control is what proves the harness can see the thing it claims to pin. pnpm bench:action-install compares a fresh run against the baseline and exits non-zero on any drift; bench:action-install:update-baseline regenerates it. Unit tests cover the pure pieces (packument shape, fixture construction, comparison) without npm or network.

Not wired into ci.yml in this change. It runs offline in about ten seconds after a build, so it could be; that is a separate decision.

Rebased onto main after #42. Typecheck and public-hygiene lint clean, full suite 1413 passing.

author: hansonfeng123
body:
# PR: Workspace auto-select, sidebar solo mode, and connection-stability fixes

## 摘要 / Summary

This PR adds **workspace auto-select** and a **sidebar solo mode** to the DSH panel, and fixes two
connection-stability problems that made the panel disconnect on its own.

It is based directly on `main` (v0.4.0) and bumps the version to **0.4.1**. The change set is
deliberately narrow: 3 commits, no unrelated refactors, no new dependencies.

---

## Why / 动机

The DSH sidebar lists **every workspace** you have ever used (one group per directory). When you open
a folder in VS Code, the extension previously used that folder only as the `dsh web` working
directory — it did **not** make the DSH sidebar follow it. So every time you switched projects you had
to find and click the matching directory in the DSH sidebar yourself.

Two independent problems also caused the panel to report the service as disconnected even though it
was perfectly alive:

1. **A start timeout that was too short.** With a plugin-heavy DSH, cold start can exceed the
   hard-coded 15 s, so the panel reported *“service not ready within 15 s”*. Pressing **Reconnect**
   worked, because by then the service had finished booting.
2. **A health probe with zero tolerance.** The ready-state probe reused the 3 s start-up timeout and
   flipped the panel to `idle` on the **first** miss. When DSH is busy (running a model, many
   plugins), a 3 s non-response is common — and the cost of a false positive is high: the usable
   iframe is replaced by the “disconnected” placeholder page.

---

## What changed / 改动

### 1. Workspace auto-select (`dsh.workspace.autoSelect`, default `true`)

When the panel opens, the extension now:

1. idempotently registers the current VS Code folder as a DSH workspace
   (`workspaces.create` reuses an existing one — never duplicates);
2. calls DSH's front-end `uiWorkspace.openWorkspace` — **the same function a sidebar click invokes** —
   so session creation/reuse, sidebar highlight and persistence behave identically to a manual click.
   If the current session already belongs to the target workspace, the extension **does not** switch,
   so an ongoing conversation is never interrupted;
3. pushes later changes (workspace switch, settings change) through a `syncWorkspace` message instead
   of reloading the page.

### 2. Sidebar solo mode (`dsh.workspace.soloMode`, default `true`)

Other workspace groups are hidden so the sidebar contains only the current project and its
conversations. This is a **purely visual** filter (`display:none`) — no data is deleted and no session
is affected. Clearing the VS Code folder or turning the setting off restores everything instantly.

### 3. Health-probe tolerance and a longer start timeout

- `startTimeoutMs`: **15 s → 45 s** (configurable via `dsh.startTimeoutMs`).
- Health probe now uses its **own** timeout (default 10 s, `healthProbeTimeoutMs`) instead of the 3 s
  start-up probe value.
- **Consecutive-failure counting**: the service is only declared dead after
  `healthCheck.failureThreshold` consecutive misses (default **3**); any success resets the counter.
  A single miss never disconnects.
- Probe interval relaxed **30 s → 120 s** (`healthCheck.intervalMs`); set it to `0` to disable probing
  entirely.
- Every failed probe is logged (`连续失败 N/3`) so it is obvious *why* a disconnect happened.

### 4. Windows fixes

- **POSIX path joining.** `findInPathPosix` / `resolveDshPackageJsonPath` joined POSIX paths with the
  platform-dependent `path.join`, producing `\usr\local\bin\dsh` on Windows and making `dsh` version
  detection always fail (also turning the cross-platform unit tests red on Windows).
  Now `findInPathPosix` always uses `path.posix`, and `resolveDshPackageJsonPath` picks
  `path.posix` / `path.win32` from the input path shape.
- **Bridge disable self-heal.** DSH can leave a stale record in the profile config
  (`cordis.patch.yml`):
  ```yaml
  # dsh-fix: disabled entry "dsh-vscode-bridge"
  - id: "dsh-vscode-bridge"
    disabled: true
  ```
  Because cordis applies later entries last, the bridge package stayed installed but **inactive**, with
  no way to recover (symptoms: external links dead, file-path clicks dead, workspace sync inert). The
  installer now clears that record on every activation, using a conservative match on the `dsh-fix`
  comment header so a user's own manual disable is never touched.

### 5. Two stability bugs introduced by this feature (fixed here as well)

- `pushWorkspaceSync` no longer calls `render()`. Re-setting `webview.html` reloads the iframe, which
  re-handshakes and triggers another sync push — an infinite loop that also starved the health probe.
- The delivery receipt now compares paths **case-insensitively with separator normalisation**. DSH
  canonicalises paths via `realpath` and may echo back lowercase (`c:/homework/...`) while the
  extension holds VS Code's original casing, so the previous strict comparison never matched and the
  retry loop never stopped.

---

## How to test / 验证

```bash
npm install
npm run typecheck   # 0 errors
npm test            # green on CI (ubuntu-latest)
npm run package     # produces dsh-vscode.vsix
```

### Test-suite status on Windows (pre-existing, not caused by this PR)

`npm run typecheck` and the feature tests pass everywhere. On **Windows**, `npm test` additionally
reports 30 failures that **already exist on `main`** and are unrelated to this change:

| Failed suite | Count | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `test/bridge/host.test.ts`, `test/bridge/installer.test.ts` | 29 | The fixtures use POSIX paths (`/home/u/.dsh`, `/proj/src/main.ts`) while the modules under test legitimately use the platform's `path.join`/`path.resolve`. On Windows the two cannot match. **The source is correct** — production always receives native paths — so the proper fix is to make those fixtures platform-aware, which is left out of this PR to keep it focused. |
| `test/integration/auth.test.ts` | 1 | A real-`dsh` integration test, gated on `DSH_HOME`. It only runs when `DSH_HOME` is set (never on CI), and it is unchanged by this PR. |

On Linux/macOS and on CI none of these occur. I did include one genuine cross-platform source fix
(`findInPathPosix` / `resolveDshPackageJsonPath`), because those two functions are documented as
POSIX-path handling and yet used the platform-dependent joiner — a real bug, not a fixture issue.

Manual verification for the two features:

1. Install the built VSIX, open a folder such as `~/projects/my-app`, click the DSH icon.
   → DSH should switch to the `my-app` workspace on its own and open its session.
2. The sidebar should show only that workspace group.
3. Switch to another folder → the panel follows.
4. Turn both settings off → the sidebar shows all groups again.
5. Health-probe tolerance: set `dsh.healthCheck.intervalMs` to `0` and use the panel; it should never
   show “disconnected” on its own. Re-enable with a long interval and repeat.

---

## Settings added / 新增设置项

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `dsh.workspace.autoSelect` | `true` | Auto-switch DSH to the workspace matching the current VS Code folder |
| `dsh.workspace.soloMode` | `true` | Show only the current workspace group in the sidebar |
| `dsh.startTimeoutMs` | `45000` | How long to wait for `dsh web` to become ready |
| `dsh.healthCheck.intervalMs` | `120000` | Interval between health probes (`0` disables) |
| `dsh.healthCheck.probeTimeoutMs` | `10000` | Timeout for a single health probe |
| `dsh.healthCheck.failureThreshold` | `3` | Consecutive failures required to report a disconnect |

---

## Risk / 风险与回退

- **Fail-open everywhere.** If the workspace cannot be matched (e.g. it was renamed inside DSH), if the
  front-end services are unavailable, or if the sidebar has not rendered yet, the extension leaves

author: fil-donadoni
body:
Slice 1 of issue #3235, which bundles three independent Avatar keyword-actions. This one ships **firebending (CR 702.189) whole**, plus its first and only card, **The Legend of Roku // Avatar Roku**. Waterbend and airbend are sliced into their own issues (linked below) with the full design walk already recorded — the user chose that split after this slice was complete.

## What changed

**Firebending N (CR 702.189).** `"Firebending N" means "Whenever this creature attacks, add N {R}. Until end of combat, you don't lose this mana as steps and phases end."` `expandFirebending` (`convex/cards/abilities/firebending.ts`) desugars the `staticAbilities` string at the `getDefinition` seam — annihilator's shape (ADR 0054) — into one `attacksTrigger` per declared instance whose whole body is the already-shipped `addMana` Op. No firebending-specific Op, no new primitive, no `resolve()`.

**A mana LIFETIME, which no engine mana had.** The issue brief's premise that a "designated-source pool that already persists past its step" existed does not hold: `RestrictedMana` is documented as emptying with the fungible pool at every CR 500.5 boundary, and a grep for a duration flag on any mana path returns nothing. So `addMana` gained ONE orthogonal optional field, `persistsUntil: ManaPersistence` (today the single member `"end-of-combat"`), threaded through `SpellContext.addManaTo` into `addRestrictedManaToPool`.

A persistent unit is the Arena of Glory shape (issue #3354): a tagged `restrictedMana` entry with **no** `restriction`, **no** `castableCardId` and **no** rider, so it stays spendable on anything — it is plain red mana that merely outlives its step. It lives in the tagged list for the mundane reason that a `Record<string, number>` count map has nowhere to record a lifetime.

`persistsUntil` joins the CR 106.4 bucket key at the deposit, and is EXCLUDED fail-closed from `reverseRestrictedManaFromPool` and both `manaBalanceForRestriction*` lookups — all three ask "is the mana this TAP produced still unspent", and a firebending unit was produced by a resolved trigger. Without the exclusion, untapping a plain Mountain before spending its `{R}` would have decremented the firebending unit instead.

The boundary is `manaPersistenceSurvives` (`gre/state.ts`), the single authority `emptyManaPools` consults: `"end-of-combat"` survives every combat STEP boundary except END_OF_COMBAT's own exit — which is also the combat PHASE's exit, since this engine models combat as six sibling `Phase` values with no separate phase token (CR 511.2 / 500.5a). It fails CLOSED outside combat, so an "end the combat phase" effect (CR 506.4) that skips past END_OF_COMBAT empties the mana at the very next boundary rather than leaving it floating for the turn.

**`exileTopOfLibrary` Op (CR 701.13 Exile / CR 406.3), the 98th.** Roku's chapter I needed "exile the top three cards of your library". A **sibling** of the mill Op, deliberately not a destination parameter on it: CR 701.17a defines milling as putting cards into the graveyard, so an Op named for that keyword action but carrying a destination would misname the very action the Mechanics Registry is the name authority for. Composition only — the same `peekLibraryTop` + per-card `moveCardById(…, "library", "exile")` pair `lookDistribute`'s exile leg already runs, plus the CR 607 `linkExileToSource` stamp `hideaway` uses. It closes the gap Elkin Bottle confesses in prose ("exile-top + cast-from-exile has no Op skin yet"). All **eight** registration sites, including `choiceDepth.RAISES_RESOLUTION_CHOICE`, which `/new-op`'s table of seven does not list.

**A third cast-from-exile window, `"until-end-of-your-next-turn"` (CR 514.2 / 608.2g).** Both shipped windows are too short: `"this-turn"` dies at this turn's cleanup, and `"until-next-end-step"` is a different boundary whose helper carries an early return that is wrong here ("your next END STEP" can be satisfied by the current turn; "your next TURN" never can). The new helper's doc says why the two must not be merged.

**The Bot could not SEE the mana.** `getLegalActions` has always folded eligible restricted mana into its affordability census (`rules.ts`); `planManaPayment` (`moves.ts`) read `player.manaPool` alone. The two authorities therefore disagreed in the direction that makes the bot WEAKER: a cast legal for a human was simply never enumerated, and the seat passed holding mana. `docs/findings/3354-…` and `docs/findings/3460-…` both call that latent **"unless a shipped restricted source ever becomes auto-tappable"** — firebending is that source, since its four red arrive from an attack trigger the bot cannot decline. `unrestrictedFloatingMana` (`gre/state.ts`) folds in the units that carry no restriction at all, at both readers (`planManaPayment` and `poolUnits`/`manaCensusFor`). Genuinely restricted units stay out: their eligibility depends on the cost being paid, and folding them in unconditionally would have the bot enumerate casts the server then refuses.

**The Legend of Roku // Avatar Roku** (`tla/red.ts`, Scryfall tla #145). Chapter II needs no "any colour mana" Op and does **not** block on issue #1368, despite the brief: that issue is about an "any colour" choice inside a MANA ABILITY, which resolves outside the stack (CR 605.1b/605.4) and cannot raise a choice at all. A Saga chapter is an ordinary triggered ability ON the stack, so the shipped `colorChoiceModes` + `addMana` composition applies unchanged. Chapter III is byte-identical to Fable of the Mirror-Breaker's own. The 4/4 Dragon token carries `firebending 4` on its own `staticAbilities`, which is what makes "grantable to a token" true by construction — `tokenDefinitionId` hashes the string into the token id and `getDefinition` runs the synthesized definition through the same expander a printed card goes through.

**Also fixed in passing:** the `play` registry row cited CR 701.13, which is *Exile* (the `exile` row already holds that number). Play is CR 701.18 — corrected against `bun run cr 701.18`, which the new Op's own 701.13 citation made visible.

**Regenerated:** card index, oracle lockfile, catalogue pack, Vintage Cube pick rating.

## Tests + proof-of-failure

New: `convex/cards/abilities/__tests__/firebending.test.ts` (15), the `exileTopOfLibrary` and window blocks in `convex/gre/effects/__tests__/interpreter.test.ts` (13), three label cases in `src/lib/__tests__/restricted-mana.test.ts`, one `must` blade entry.

Every guarding test proven to fail — break, watch red, revert, all reverts verified clean:

| Broke | Red |
| --- | --- |
| `manaPersistenceSurvives` → always `false` | 2 failed / 13 passed |
| `emptyManaPools` spares nothing | 1 failed / 14 passed |
| dropped the `persistsUntil === undefined` exclusion from `reverseRestrictedManaFromPool` | 1 failed / 14 passed |
| `restrictedManaLabel` drops the lifetime clause | 1 failed / 14 passed |
| `expandFirebending` unwired from the `getDefinition` chain | 7 failed / 8 passed |
| `planManaPayment` stops seeing unrestricted floating mana | blade `must` red — `seed 727774: chose [pass]` |

The last one is the discriminating proof for the bot half: without the fix the blade entry's bot passes while holding exactly enough mana to cast.

## Bot reachability

- **`enumerateMoves`** — firebending is a triggered ability (auto-stacked, no Move). Avatar Roku's `{8}` is a plain `cost.mana` activated ability, reached by `enumerateAbilityMoves` with no new cost shape. `exileTopOfLibrary` runs inside a chapter's resolution, never as a Move.

author: juliush-dev
body:
## What this is

Four rules, each bought by a failure in a real document, plus the one small kit change
that makes the first of them fixable rather than merely documentable. The document was
`sites/library-use` (a published app-shell scene); every failure below shipped with
`check/verify.mjs` reporting **all 6 configurations hold**.

## The four failures

| # | What happened | Why nothing caught it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Two of six cards wore their **Enter mark in the air above the card** | The harness compares the mark with the object's bounds, and an object's bounds are everything its `draw` put in the group — including the row heading that raised them |
| 2 | The **reading panel blanked** on entering a level; in the same handler, root-level flow arrows stayed drawn over the interior | `onPick(null, {depth:true})` is the kit reporting a level change; clearing on every null call wipes the panel at the moment the reader goes in, and an early return skips whatever else the handler does |
| 3 | **Arrow labels half-swallowed by the cards** either side — a first letter on one card, a last letter on the other | A labels layer created before the content is painted underneath it; a label too wide for its gap is covered, not clipped, and nothing warns |
| 4 | A substage read **1,3,5 then 2,4** while the index beside it listed **1,2,3,4,5** | A two-column grid whose row gap (15) was smaller than its column gap (40) groups by column. The reader asked the only question the layout left open and answered it the way the spacing told them to |

Number 4 was found by a reader of the published page, not by a check; 1 and 3 the same.

## What the PR does

**Kit change — `partials/stage.js`.** The Enter mark anchors to `[data-face]` when an
object declares one, falling back to the object's group. One object can then carry a
heading, a caption or a badge without moving its door. Backwards compatible: no
`data-face`, same behaviour as before.

**`LAWS.md`.** In 7a: *one hierarchy, one order* — the stage reads in the index's order,
top to bottom then left to right, and where the contents are a list, draw them as a list.
Plus a bullet on the mark: it pins to the **face**, not to everything in its group.

**`TRAPS.md`.** Three authoring traps (decoration inside an object group lifts the mark;
`onPick(null, {depth:true})` is a level change, not a deselect, so the guard must not
swallow the handler's other work; a layer under the objects hides whatever does not fit
between them) and one checking trap (`#content` is not the live level one level down —
it keeps the root drawing, so a query at depth returns zero-size rects and reads as
"nothing is drawn" rather than "wrong layer").

**`README.md`.** Documents the `data-face` convention where the Enter control is described.

**`check/`.** Three executable assertions, each shown failing against the broken case:

- `affordances.mjs` — the mark is asserted against the object's **face** where declared,
  and a new regression test grows an object a heading outside its shape and asserts the
  mark did not move with it.
- `verify.mjs` — two rules. *One order*: a level's objects must be readable in the order
  the index gives them, where the stage presents them as a grid. A grid offers two readings
  (by row, by column); the rule fails when the index matches neither, and when it matches
  the one the gaps do not favour — but only where the layout really is a grid, and only
  where the gaps decide it (1.5:1, chosen for legibility, not measured). *Nothing painted
  under an object*: text drawn outside the objects must not be covered by one, with a
  level's own labels excluded so a faded level's drawing is not reported.

## Evidence

Each new assertion was run against a deliberately broken build, and the whole set was
re-run against every document that depends on the kit:

| Broken build | Result |
|---|---|
| `check/affordances` with the pre-fix anchoring (mark on the group) | **fails** — `Enter Server left its face when its object grew a heading` |
| a scratch model whose two outer cards are drawn in the opposite order to the index | **fails** — `order: the index lists the level in an order the stage does not offer` |
| a scratch grid 100 across, 20 down, with a row-major index | **fails** — `order: the stage groups by column while the index reads by row` |
| a scratch model whose sibling label layer overlaps a card | **fails** — `order: "a label wider than" is drawn outside the objects but painted under one` |

**The order rule was written wrong three times, and the controls caught it every time.**
Worth recording, because each wrong version looked reasonable:

1. Sorting by top-then-left and comparing to the index reported `sites/library` — a document
   that reads *by column*, with an index that agrees with that reading. A rule that fails a
   correct document is worse than no rule.
2. Comparing both readings against the gaps then reported `sites/ssh-arch`, whose root level
   is a free-form network diagram: seven nodes at scattered coordinates give seven "rows" and
   six "columns", and a gap between "the first two lefts" is then a gap between two objects
   that merely happen to be leftmost of each. Fixed by requiring the layout to be grid-like
   (`rows × columns ≤ objects + 2`). The same run also flagged an unambiguous L-shape whose
   two readings coincide — where the space offers exactly one order, the gaps cannot pick the
   wrong one.
3. It then reported `sites/elements`, whose panels sit two columns apart with **20 pixels
   between columns and 19 between rows** — a rounding difference, not a grouping. Fixed by
   requiring the gaps to be decisive.

The final rule fires on all four broken builds above and passes every document on this box.

After the changes, with every example rebuilt from the new partials:

```
check                   all 6 configurations hold
check:model             stage model: all 6 configurations hold
check:affordances       entry affordances: all 6 configurations hold
check:depth             depth transitions: all 6 configurations hold
check:context           Context checks passed: 6 viewport/motion configurations.
check:enter-motion      entry motion: all 6 configurations hold
```

Every dependent document was rebuilt (the sites in `~/sites`) and re-verified.

## Two measuring instruments that lied, worth knowing

Both are now in `TRAPS.md` under the checking section:

- **Nearest-neighbour by centre distance** says a plate directly below is closer than the
  next plate across (342px vs 396px) even when the gaps are 96 across and 192 down.
  Proximity for boxes is the gap between edges, not centre distance.
- **Nearest-neighbour at all, on a grid**: with a 40 unit column gap and a 96 unit row
  gap, an item's diagonal neighbour (≈104) is farther than the item below it in the same
  column (96), so "each item's nearest neighbour must be its index neighbour" fails on a
  layout no reader would misread. The sufficient condition is the gap comparison.

The general shape, and the reason these belong in the kit's own record rather than a
session: **the kit measures the object you declared, not the thing the reader sees.**

author: chrisgeo
body:
## Summary

`go-api-prove` needs a fresh effective-principal envelope to authenticate against `query-api`. Rather than asking a running `api` pod for one over the network (the design this PR started with — superseded), the tools pod now mints it **locally**: it already receives the same Ed25519 signing key material the `api` pod's environment holds, via the same Secret key mounted the same way (`secretKeyRef`), so nothing new touches the network and no new credential class is introduced.

- `internal/envelopemint` carries the signing logic — a `Claims` struct kept field-for-field identical to `cmd/query-api/internal/principal.Claims` and `principal_envelope.EffectivePrincipalEnvelopeClaims` (can't import the former directly: it's `internal/` scoped to `cmd/query-api`), `LoadPrivateKey`/`LoadPrivateKeyFromEnv` (PKCS#8 PEM, same shape `GO_API_ENVELOPE_PRIVATE_KEY` already takes), and `Mint`/`MintProveEnvelope` (fixed synthetic superuser principal scoped to the caller's `-org`, TTL 60s, same env-var-overridable issuer/audience/kid names `principal_envelope.py` uses).
- `cmd/mint-envelope` is the small binary the tools image ships as `go-api-prove`'s `-proof-bearer-exec` helper: reads the key from `GO_API_ENVELOPE_PRIVATE_KEY` by env var name (never argv), or `-key-file` for local/dev use, and prints the raw envelope to stdout only.
- `cmd/query-api/internal/principal/envelopemint_compat_test.go` proves byte-compatibility: it signs with `internal/envelopemint` and verifies with the REAL `principal.Verifier` — not a self-consistent Go-only fixture. Lives under `cmd/query-api/internal/principal` because that's the only direction Go's own `internal/` visibility rule allows (envelopemint cannot import back into it). The pre-existing `TestVerifierMatchesLivePythonIssuedEnvelope` (Python issuer ↔ Go verifier) is untouched and still covers that separate compatibility axis.
- `docker/go-api-tools.Dockerfile` builds and ships `mint-envelope` alongside `go-api-routing`/`go-api-prove`.
- Docs (`go-api-wave-0-proof-infrastructure.md`, `query-api-bootstrap.md`) updated: the `kubectl run`/`go-api-prove` examples now show `GO_API_ENVELOPE_PRIVATE_KEY` reaching the tools Pod via `secretKeyRef` (matching the shape proven on prod for JOB 7), never a copied key file.

No Python or API-surface changes — the earlier internal route, its tests, and the endpoint-profile/credential-class contract recount are all reverted; the api gains nothing here.

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./... && go vet ./internal/... ./cmd/...`
- [x] `go test ./cmd/go-api-prove/... ./cmd/go-api-routing/... ./internal/goapiproof/... ./cmd/mint-envelope/... ./internal/envelopemint/... ./cmd/query-api/internal/principal/... -count=1` — all pass, no regression, including the new sign-with-envelopemint/verify-with-Verifier compat tests
- [x] `ci/check_go.sh fmt` / `ci/check_go.sh vet` — clean
- [x] No Python files touched by this branch — the earlier `ci/local_validate.sh` gate result from the prior (superseded) design carries: nothing in this diff is a Python-gate input

author: raykavin
body:
`respond.Error` hardcoded the internal-error text for every status, so a 422 or a 404 sent through it arrived describing itself as an internal server failure:

```json
{ "success": false, "message": "An internal server error occurred", "errors": [ ... ] }
```

That contradicts the status code on the wire, and it is the message a client with no mapping for the error's `code` falls back to. It also made `respond.Error` behave differently from the dedicated helper for the same status — which matters because the `ErrorResolver` path always goes through `respond.Error`.

Picks the default envelope message from the status instead, matching what `BadRequest`, `NotFound`, `UnprocessableEntity` and friends would have sent. Anything unmapped keeps the internal-error text.

author: kingye
body:
## What

Add two slash commands that toggle one skill / MCP server on or off **for a single topic at runtime**, without editing config or restarting:

```
/skill on|off|reset <name>   # persisted in .jyc/skill-override.json
/mcp   on|off|reset <name>   # persisted in .jyc/mcp-override.json
```

- `on`: force-enable (un-disable `disabled_mcps` / join the skill whitelist even if config excluded it)
- `off`: force-disable (even if whitelisted by config)
- `reset`: clear the override, back to config defaults
- Takes effect from the next message (tool registry + system prompt are rebuilt per message); persists across restarts until explicit reset — same lifecycle as `/model`, `/mode`, `/context`.

## How

- `session_state::ToggleOverride` + read/write/clear helpers (shared file format `{"on":[],"off":[]}`)
- One parameterized `ToggleCommandHandler` serves both commands (only the `on` validator differs: `/skill` checks `SKILL.md` exists in the discovery roots, `/mcp` checks the server is defined in any config layer)
- `tools.rs`: apply `/mcp` override to the effective `disabled_mcps`
- `prompt.rs`: merge `/skill` override into the include/exclude lists fed to `discover_skills`

Part of the MCP-context-size investigation: enables auditing big MCP servers (e.g. `jin_full_mcp`) by switching them on only in topics that need them.

body:
Heeler now runs natively on iPad with an adaptive two-column Console, hardware keyboard commands, Composer drag and drop, and multiple windows. The shared Terminal keyboard fills the available dock width while preserving its height and consistent character-key sizing.

## Changes

- Restore iPad support for the app and extensions, all four iPad orientations, adaptive sheets/popovers, and persistent sidebar presentation.
- Add scene-scoped keyboard commands and Agent windows with restoration, notification routing, and explicit same-Host terminal handover. Coalesce terminal resize reports during live window resizing.
- Stage dropped text and images in Composer, preserving insertion order and preventing submission while images are uploading.
- Use one shortcut strip and an icon to switch Composer/Direct Input on every device. Align the More button with adjacent keys and adapt the full Terminal keyboard to its dock width.
- Repair keyboard inset handoffs, terminal rendering scale after resizing, and first-responder release under the three iPad keyboard docks.
- Add `make sim-ipad`, `make test-ipad`, and `make install-ipad`, including physical-device registration during installation. Include the regenerated Xcode project and the iPad acceptance report.

## Validation

- At integration candidate `1b6c792`, the committed acceptance report records full `make test`: 1,811 app tests across 169 suites and 49 HeelerSSH package tests. author: jerryfane
body:
Closes #2171. Authority: owner assignment recorded in workflow note 147740.

## What a seat does now

```sh
gitmoot review request --pr 2170            # Gitmoot picks reviewer/runtime/model, dedups, wakes you
gitmoot review status  --pr 2170
```

## Behavior

- **Atomic dedup on (repo, PR, exact head, purpose)** — new `review_requests` table; the PRIMARY KEY insert is the claim. Concurrent requesters get `attached` to the one job; a saved `approved`/`changes_requested` verdict returns `verdict_exists` and spends nothing; a claim standing on a job that ended without a verdict (including the daemon's synthetic `failed` recovery result) is taken over by the next requester. A different purpose is a different question.
- **OMP default with per-purpose ordered model pools** — `[review_router] code|security|ui|architecture = ["provider/model", ...]`; provider-qualified, validated at load. Job runs as background review-only (`no_fix_target`) on `omp` with a fresh per-job session on a review-capable, non-implement agent scoped to the repo.
- **Operational fallback before any verdict** — in the existing `deferOperationalBlockerPreTerminal` seam: quota, auth, or an omp *provider stream stall* (measured live: `omp turn failed (stopReason error): Provider stream stalled while waiting for the next event`, previously unclassified → terminal fail) advances `payload.Model` to the next pool entry and re-queues immediately (`review_model_fallback` event). Exhausted pool → ordinary timed hold; shared attempt budget bounds it. A verdict never changes the model.
- **Requester wake independent of gate advancement** — reuses `awaited_facts` + `wake_outbox`: the router subscribes the requesting org role to the exact-head verdict; satisfaction happens inside the reviewing job's state-transition transaction. The satisfaction wake now carries the resolution detail (decision, findings count, executed-check count, evidence declaration, `gitmoot job show <id>`), so the requester reads the answer from the prompt. Same-role duplicate requests keep the original wait.
- **Honest holds** — request output names daemon-not-running / disk-guard-paused at dispatch time; `review status` shows per-job hold reason from the stuck-reason surface.

## Verification (executed)

- `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestReviewRequest|TestReviewModelPool'`: dedup/attach/purpose-split/resultless-and-synthetic-failure reclaim/verdict-reuse with satisfied fact; claim release on reviewer refusal; pool fallback through the real `runQueuedJobsForRepo → Mailbox.Run → deferrer` path for provider-stall then 429 (immediate re-queue, then timed hold).
- `go test ./internal/config -run TestReviewRouter`, `./internal/db` (migration-upgrade marker updated to `idx_review_requests_job`), `./internal/workflow`, `./skills`, `go vet ./...` — green. Full `./internal/cli` and `./internal/db` reruns from a clean tree in progress at time of opening; result will be posted.
- **Live smoke** in an isolated home with this binary against PR #2167: `review request` resolved the head from GitHub, claimed, dispatched on `omp`/`devin/swe-2` in a Landlock read-only seat; duplicate request → `attached`; a resultless failure and a synthetic-failed recovery both yielded the claim to the next request; the verdict (approved, 2 findings) satisfied the awaited fact at persistence time and the wake was delivered to the requesting role's pane by the outbox drain.

## Not in this PR

- No deployment; the production daemon still runs the pre-router binary.
- Merge-gate family predicate (#2169), advancement race (#2170), OMP seat approvals (#2167) are separate PRs; this change integrates with their reviewed contracts rather than copying them.
- Machine-local `AGENTS.md` guidance to prefer `gitmoot review request` follows deployment.

author: jdmorgenstein
body:
## The problem

Goal: one iCloud library holding every unique photo from iCloud **and** Google Photos, including the photo-shoot albums that only ever existed in Google, with no duplicates — so Google Photos can be cancelled.

The obstacle is real: **file hashes cannot identify the same photo across the two libraries.** Four causes, and they stack:

| Cause | Changes | Pixels identical? |
|---|---|---|
| Takeout rewrites metadata into JSON sidecars, stripping it from the file | bytes | **yes** |
| "Storage saver" resizes anything over 16 MP and re-compresses | bytes + pixels | no |
| HEIC → JPEG transcoding on some upload paths | bytes + pixels | no |
| An edit applied on one side only | bytes + pixels | no |

Row 1 is the common case: bit-for-bit the same photograph, and SHA-256 still disagrees.

## The approach

Identity comes from the **capture**, not the bytes. The matcher runs a cascade, strongest evidence first, stopping at the first tier that fires:

1. **Apple `ContentIdentifier`** (EXIF `MakerNotes` tag `0x0011`) — a per-capture UUID the iPhone writes, which survives any re-encode that carries EXIF through. Exact, zero false-positive risk, and the signal most tools miss.
2. **File SHA-256** — free and exact when nothing was touched.
3. **SHA-256 of the decoded, orientation-normalised RGB buffer** — the direct answer to "the hashes differ". Decode both and hash the *pixels*, and a metadata-only rewrite collapses to an exact match. Still exact.
4. **Sub-second EXIF capture instant + pHash/dHash** — for genuine re-encodes, where the pixels really do differ.
5. **Perceptual evidence alone** → review queue, never deletion.

## Why tier 5 is held back

Measured on the bundled fixtures: a frame shifted a few pixels — what the next shot in a burst looks like — sits at pHash distance **0–6** (median 2). A re-encode of a single photo sits in that same band. Two genuinely different photos sit at **22–44**.

So perceptual distance alone cannot separate "re-encoded copy" from "next burst frame" at *any* threshold. A pHash-only dedupe silently deletes burst frames, panorama sequences and near-duplicate portraits — unrecoverable once Google Photos is gone.

What separates them is the sub-second capture time and `BurstUUID` (Apple maker note `0x000B`), so tiers 4 and 5 additionally require agreement on sub-second capture time, burst id, camera model and aspect ratio.

The whole design follows one asymmetry: **missing a duplicate costs storage; a false duplicate costs a photograph.**

## Scale

Benchmarked at 120k iCloud × 150k Google rows, `match` originally did not finish in ten minutes. The banded perceptual index was the cause and was worse than useless: banding a 64-bit hash for a Hamming threshold of 6 needs 7 bands of ~9 bits, so at most 512 buckets — at 120k photos every bucket is populated and the index filters nothing. The dHash index was banded for threshold 12 (13 bands of ~5 bits, 400 buckets, ~3,900 rows each), putting ~52k candidates into every query.

Candidate generation is now split by what each tier actually asks:

- **Tier 4 blocks on capture time.** It already insists on an identical capture instant, so the timestamp is the natural key — an exact lookup returning a handful of rows, with the perceptual hashes only confirming.
- **Tier 5 blocks on banded pHash** at the strict tier-5 threshold (4 → five bands of ~13 bits → 36k buckets, ~16 rows each), where the pigeonhole guarantee still buys selectivity.
- **The dHash index is gone.** `scan` computes both hashes together or neither, so dHash bands reach no candidate pHash bands miss.

Same benchmark, worst case (random hashes, no matches, so every row falls through every tier): **18.3s, 552 MB peak.**

## Two-pass indexing

Most of the cost is decoding images, but tiers 1 and 2 need no pixels at all. `index --quick` skips the decode and keeps the metadata (`Image.open` reads header and EXIF without touching pixels, so the `ContentIdentifier` still comes back on every file). `index --upgrade` then decodes only what `match` could not settle.

Measured on 12 MP JPEGs averaging 5.8 MB: **243 files/second/core quick vs 3.7 full**, and I/O bound rather than CPU bound.

An acceptance test asserts the two-pass route reaches identical verdicts to a full index. The first version of the upgrade selection used "has no capture time" to identify the files tier 3 exists for — wrong, because Takeout supplies a capture time from the JSON sidecar even where it stripped the EXIF, so every metadata-stripped file was skipped and 20 duplicates went undetected. That test is what caught it.

## Takeout handling

- All known sidecar naming variants — `.json`, `.supplemental-metadata.json`, truncated forms (`.supplemental-metad.json`, `.s.json`), numbered duplicates (`IMG_1.jpg.supplemental-metadata(1).json`), `-edited` derivatives — with each sidecar's own `title` field as an authoritative fallback index.
- Album folders distinguished from `Photos from YYYY` and other system folders.
- Takeout's internal duplication (a photo copied into every album folder *and* the year folder) collapsed at report time, with album membership unioned.
- Live Photo halves kept together: if either the still or the clip is unique, both are kept, and staged names keep a shared stem so `osxphotos import --auto-live` can re-pair them.

## Album reconstruction

`stage --rebuild-albums` also stages the **iCloud original** of every album member iCloud already has. Those files are byte-identical to what Photos stores, so `osxphotos import --skip-dups --dup-albums` recognises them by Photos' own fingerprint, imports nothing, and adds the *existing* photo to the album. That reproduces each Google album in full — old and new photos together — without creating a single duplicate asset.

## Pre-flight

`photodedup doctor` checks exiftool, HEIC decoding and numpy, surveys both exports with an indexing time estimate, verifies free disk against the staging tree, and samples the Takeout for sidecar coverage. Low coverage means not every archive part was extracted — which would make whole albums look unique and import thousands of duplicates.

## Usage

```bash
python -m photodedup doctor --icloud ~/export/icloud --google "~/export/Takeout/Google Photos"
python -m photodedup index  --library icloud --root ~/export/icloud --quick
python -m photodedup index  --library google --root "~/export/Takeout/Google Photos" --takeout --quick
python -m photodedup match
python -m photodedup index  --library icloud --root ~/export/icloud --upgrade
python -m photodedup index  --library google --root "~/export/Takeout/Google Photos" --takeout --upgrade
python -m photodedup match
python -m photodedup report --out ~/export/report      # read this before changing anything
python -m photodedup stage  --out ~/export/staging --rebuild-albums
python -m photodedup plan   --staging ~/export/staging --rebuild-albums
```

Nothing is ever deleted; staging only hard-links.

## Testing

**45 tests, all passing.** Includes a full synthetic migration (byte-identical copies, metadata-stripped copies, Storage saver re-encodes, Google-only album photos, Live Photo pairs, incremental re-scan, album rebuilding, the burst false-positive guard), band-selectivity regression tests for the scale bug, and the two-pass equivalence acceptance test. Verified end-to-end through the CLI on a 144-file synthetic library; the pure-Python and numpy DCT paths verified bit-identical across 40 images.

A bug the new tests caught: `_capture_only_match` did not check media kind, so a still could be declared a duplicate of a clip sharing its sub-second capture time — exactly what a Live Photo pair looks like.

## Why there is no API route

Documented in the README with sources:

- Google Photos **Library API** read scopes were removed 31 March 2025 (`403 PERMISSION_DENIED`).
- The **Picker API** cannot enumerate a library, and its `=d` download withholds GPS, drops metadata and returns a re-encode — strippi

author: pieer
body:
## What

Markdown typed or pasted into the Toast UI Visual (WYSIWYG) editor was committed backslash-escaped (`\# Heading`, `\**bold**`, `` \```mermaid ``), so it rendered as literal text on the Read tab and showed up escaped in the Source editor. This is the shared root cause of #322 and of the remaining open piece of #367 (escaped ```` ```mermaid ```` fences breaking diagram rendering; the codeblock toolbar button itself was already restored by #372).

Closes #322
Closes #367

## How (real fix, not the notice fallback)

Product decision: markdown-looking input typed in the Visual editor is markdown. Rather than showing a "use the Source editor" notice, the escapes are removed so the input is interpreted:

- `unescapeTypedMarkdown.ts` (new): removes the WYSIWYG serializer's backslash escapes, code-aware — fenced code block content and inline code spans stay verbatim (a `\d` in real code is user content). Fences are tracked as they form: an escaped `` \```mermaid `` line unescapes into a real opening fence and protects its body; a still-escaped closing line ends the block.
- `markdownThreeWayMerge.ts`: the merge now reports per-line provenance (`MergeStats.adoptedLines`) — which output lines came from the user's Visual edit vs. the pristine source.
- `losslessMarkdown.ts`: after resolving a Visual edit (merged, or the wholesale-serialization fallback), unescapes exactly the adopted lines. Untouched lines keep their pristine bytes, so the #262 lossless guarantees — including deliberate `\*` escapes written in Source mode — are unchanged.

Both the article editor (`toast-editor.ts`) and the comment editor (`ToastCommentEditor.ts`) share the tracker, so both are fixed.

Nice side effect: editing the sentence that holds a reference link no longer breaks that link — the re-serialized line is unescaped, so `[text][1]` keeps rendering.

## Tests

- New unit suite `unescapeTypedMarkdown.test.ts` (15 tests: escapes, code spans, fence formation/closing, tilde fences, provenance protection).
- Real-Toast-UI regression tests in `losslessMarkdown.editor.test.ts`: typing a ```` ```mermaid ```` fence as plain paragraphs in Visual mode commits a real fence (#367); typed heading/bold markdown commits unescaped (#322).
- Four existing tests that pinned the old escaped output updated to the new expectations.
- Full vitest suite passes (207 tests), eslint and vue-tsc clean.

author: dragonnite1221-lgtm
body:
## Summary

P1 finding `codegraph-2`: `runIndexFiles` in `src/indexing-operations.ts` released the cross-process file lock before indexing actually finished.

**Root cause**

```ts
try {
  return deps.orchestrator.indexFiles(filePaths); // not awaited
} finally {
  deps.fileLock.release();
}
```

Returning a promise from inside a `try` block completes that block (and therefore runs `finally`) as soon as the promise object exists, not when it settles. So `fileLock.release()` ran immediately, while the orchestrator's async `stat`/`readFile`/parse/DB-write work for the target files was still in flight. A second process (CLI, git hook, MCP server) holding no other lock could then acquire the same project lock and start writing to the same database concurrently. This is deterministic (missing `await`), not a rare interleaving — every call to `indexFiles` released the lock too early.

`runIndexAll` and `runSync` in the same file already `await` before their own `finally`, so they were unaffected.

## Fix

Add the missing `await`:

```ts
return await deps.orchestrator.indexFiles(filePaths);
```

## Test plan

- [x] Added `__tests__/index-files-lock-release.test.ts`: drives `runIndexFiles` with a real `FileLock`/`Mutex` and a fake orchestrator whose `indexFiles()` returns a controllable deferred promise. Asserts the lock file still exists while that promise is pending, and is removed only after it resolves. Deterministic — no timing/sleep dependency.
- [x] Confirmed RED against the pre-fix code (`git stash` the fix, test fails: lock file already gone while "indexing" is still pending).
- [x] Confirmed GREEN with the fix applied.
- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- [x] Existing test suite unaffected by this change (ran full `vitest run` on the combined branch; see PR description context in sibling PRs for the other two findings from the same review pass).

author: mister-guiiug
body:
Monte `@mister-guiiug/dev-pwa-config` en `^4.13.0`.

Trois versions arrivent d'un coup :

| Version | Ce qu'elle apporte |
| --- | --- |
| 4.12.1 | Node 26 ne recopie plus le `localStorage` de jsdom — le socle installait une `Map`, si bien que `Object.keys(localStorage)` rendait les NOMS DES MÉTHODES |
| 4.12.2 | `pwa-icons` crée son dossier de sortie : viser `--out public/icons` échouait sur un message de `sharp` qui ne nomme pas le dossier manquant |
| 4.13.0 | `pwa-icons` produit `apple-touch-icon.png` par défaut, en 180×180 et **opaque** — iOS ignore la transparence et compose l'alpha sur du noir |

Rien ne change sans une exécution de `npm run icons` : les deux correctifs
d'icônes portent sur le générateur, pas sur le build. La montée est donc sans
effet visible ici tant que les icônes ne sont pas régénérées.

Le `package-lock.json` est régénéré par `--package-lock-only` et non par un
`npm install` complet : sous Windows celui-ci omet les entrées optionnelles des
autres plates-formes et casse `npm ci` en CI Linux.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Dev-only dependency and lockfile update; no runtime or app source changes in the diff.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Monte le socle PWA** `@mister-guiiug/dev-pwa-config` de `^4.11.0` à `^4.13.0`, avec régénération ciblée du `package-lock.json` (`--package-lock-only`).
> 
> Les versions embarquées couvrent surtout l’outillage et les tests : correctif **jsdom / `localStorage` sous Node 26** (4.12.1), **`pwa-icons` crée le dossier de sortie** (4.12.2), et génération par défaut d’**`apple-touch-icon.png` 180×180 opaque** (4.13.0). Le lockfile reflète aussi des **peer ranges élargies** pour `vitest` et `@vitest/browser` (^5).
> 
> **Aucun changement applicatif** dans ce diff : les effets visibles sur les icônes n’apparaissent qu’après un `npm run icons` ; le build et la CI héritent surtout des scripts partagés (`pwa-bundle-budget`, `pwa-doctor`, workflow réutilisable).

body:
## Summary

Replaces the five hand-rolled button-styled `<Link>` elements (M27 audit **H2**) with `LinkButton` (the Button/Link composition fixed in #253), so built-in `variant`/`size` props drive styling instead of per-site class strings — per the audit rules *use existing components; built-in variants first; className for layout only*.

| Site | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `routes/dashboard.tsx` degraded-pool alert CTA | `bg-destructive … text-white` | `variant="destructive" size="sm"` |
| `routes/pools.tsx` header "+ Add Runner Pool" | `bg-primary text-white`, **no-op hover** | default variant (hover now works) |
| `routes/pools.tsx` warning-banner CTA | `bg-warning … text-white` | `size="sm"` + solid warning colors as `className` (see below) |
| `routes/pools.tsx` empty-state CTA | `bg-primary … text-xs` | `size="xs"` (parity with sibling `Button`) |
| `pool-diagnostics-card.tsx` remediation CTA | `bg-destructive … text-white` | `variant="destructive" size="sm"` |

### LinkButton: className now merges via Button

`LinkButton` previously forwarded `className` through `<Link>`; Base UI concatenates classes **without tailwind-merge**, so a color override (`bg-warning`) would coexist with the variant's `bg-primary` and CSS source order would decide the winner. `className` is now routed through `Button`'s `cn()`, giving proper override semantics — verified by a new regression test that failed before the routing change (it caught the substring-vs-token pitfall too).

### Deliberate deferral

The warning-banner CTA keeps `bg-warning text-white hover:bg-warning/90` as `className`: no `warning` Button variant exists and `--warning-foreground` lands in RUN-190 (H3, next in the fix order). A comment in code marks the spot; four of the five sites fully drop `text-white` here.

- E2E exercised first: `make test-e2e` — **16/16 passed** (49.1s), including the dashboard/pools flows covering all changed pages.
- Full gates: `make test && make test-scripts && make test-web && make lint && make lint-web && make vet && make build && shellcheck && shfmt && hadolint` — **exit 0**.
- `make test-web`: 146 passed (145 existing + 1 new regression test).

Closes RUN-189.

author: pakkof13-a11y
body:
## JOU-02 — taux FX de la saisie manuelle

**Root cause** : `components/modals/transaction-modal.tsx` ne rechargeait le taux **historique** (Frankfurter/BCE à la date de l'opération) que pour les types revenus (`isIncome` : DIVIDENDE/COUPON/LOYER/INTERET). Pour ACHAT/VENTE/APPORT/RETRAIT/FRAIS/REWARD/AIRDROP, un changement de devise posait le taux **du jour de la saisie** — une vraie valeur numérique — qui traversait `resolveFx()` côté serveur sans être recalculée (déjà corrigé au lot P0 pour distinguer "1"/vide de "fourni", mais aveugle à un taux fourni par erreur du formulaire plutôt que par l'utilisateur).

**Mesure sur le compte demo staging** (finance-metier, lecture seule) :

| Ligne demo | Natif | fx BCE à la date | fx spot du jour | Écart |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| APPORT USD, 2021-09-19 | 45 000 USD | 0.8489 | 0.86266 | +1,62 % / +619,20 € |
| ACHAT CHF, 2021-03-12 | 2 952,38 CHF | 0.90139 | 1.0581 | **+17,39 % / +462,67 €** |

**Correctif** :
- L'effet "taux historique" s'applique désormais à tous les types (retrait de la garde `!isIncome`) ; il redéclenche déjà sur changement de devise **et** de date en édition (`paymentDate`/`occurredAt` étaient déjà ses dépendances).
- L'effet "changement de devise" ne pose plus jamais le taux du jour dans `fxRateToEur` : `"1"` pour l'EUR, `""` sinon — le champ persisté redevient la responsabilité exclusive de l'effet historique. Le taux du jour ne sert plus qu'à la conversion optionnelle des montants (`convertAmounts`), fonctionnalité séparée et déjà connue comme approximative.
- Échec de fetch (historique ou taux du jour) : le champ reste vide, jamais de valeur fabriquée ou résiduelle d'une devise précédente, avec un hint explicite dans les deux effets.

**STOP non codé, remonté séparément (JOU-02-bis)** : `app/lib/zerion/ledger-sync.ts` et `app/lib/market/solana-ledger-sync.ts` valorisent un historique on-chain au prix et au taux **du jour de l'import**, pas à la date de la transaction on-chain — même classe de bug, hors mandat de ce lot (`crypto-onchain` / `connectors-exchanges`).

**Point produit remonté, non tranché** : le bloc `convertAmounts` convertit `unitPrice/cashAmount/fees` au taux du jour même pour une ligne datée dans le passé — décision d'ergonomie à trancher séparément.

## API-W-01 — événements DeFi, accru après validation

**Déjà corrigé et testé** dans un commit antérieur (`472aad6`, lot A), ancêtre de ce HEAD. Vérifié, rien réécrit :
- `claimReward` + `recordEvent` commettent dans une seule `prisma.$transaction` — un rejet de l'un annule l'autre.
- La date est validée par zod (`eventSchema`) avant tout accès Prisma.
